analysis.one_liner: Makes willful robocall violations a federal crime and doubles caller-ID spoofing fines.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after being introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in November 2023, it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would crack down on illegal robocalls and scam calls. It would make willful violations of the Telephone Consumer Protection Act a federal crime — up to one year in prison, or up to three years for repeat offenders, mega-volume operations (over 100,000 calls in a day, for example), calls tied to felonies, or schemes costing victims $5,000 or more. It would also double the maximum fines for providing inaccurate caller ID information, from $10,000 to $20,000. The bill never advanced past its first referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone whose phones are flooded with illegal robocalls, spoofed caller IDs, and scam calls. The new criminal penalties would apply to the people who willfully place those calls, including large-scale operations and schemes that steal money from victims, and the doubled caller-ID fines would raise the price of spoofing phone numbers to disguise where a call comes from.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds criminal penalties to the Telephone Consumer Protection Act for the first time: willful and knowing violators would face up to one year in prison, and up to three years for repeat offenders, operations placing over 100,000 calls in a day (or millions more over longer periods), calls made in furtherance of a felony, or schemes causing victims $5,000 or more in annual losses.
It doubles the maximum penalty for providing inaccurate caller identification information from $10,000 to $20,000, targeting the spoofing that makes scam calls look local or legitimate.

analysis.who_pays: Robocall operators, telemarketers, and scam callers who willfully violate the law would face prison time and doubled fines. Legitimate businesses that call or text customers bear a cost only if they act willfully and knowingly, since the criminal penalties require intent.

drawbacks.text: Criminal enforcement puts priority on prosecuting callers, but a prison sentence does not put money back in the pockets of scam victims the way civil penalties and restitution can; the bill does not add a victim-compensation mechanism.

The doubled caller-ID fines raise the ceiling on per-violation penalties, which critics of the TCPA's current enforcement regime argue can create outsized liability for call-heavy businesses; the bill's intent requirement (willful and knowing violations) narrows but does not eliminate disputes over compliance mistakes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits fall on everyone who owns a phone, since illegal robocalls and spoofed scam calls are a widespread nuisance and a vehicle for fraud, and deterrence — the realistic threat of prison for large operators — is a tool the current civil-penalty system lacks. The costs fall on the operators of illegal calling schemes, with legitimate callers largely protected by the willfulness requirement. The main design weakness is that criminal punishment alone does not compensate victims of scam losses.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to its Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cortez Masto introduced the DO NOT Call Act on November 15, 2023, joined by three original cosponsors.

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation that same day; no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in its action history.
The bill ended the 118th Congress without ever reaching the Senate floor, a routine fate for the large majority of bills referred to committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Illegal robocall and scam-call operators, who face no new criminal exposure or doubled spoofing fines because the bill never became law. Phone users keep living with the call volume the bill was meant to deter.

for.name: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto
for.role: Lead sponsor, U.S. Senator from Nevada
for.what_they_did: Introduced the DO NOT Call Act and sought criminal penalties and doubled fines for willful robocall and caller-ID spoofing violations.

for.name: Sens. Maggie Hassan, Amy Klobuchar, and Kirsten Gillibrand
Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Added a cosponsorship to the bill, one of four total.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — for the remainder of the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote ever occurred. The bill's four cosponsors were all Democrats or an Independent-aligned senator; no Republican cosponsor signed on, but no Republican opposed it on the record either, because the bill never moved.

industries.note: The bill would give these operators their first criminal exposure under the TCPA, with prison terms scaled to call volume and victim losses, plus doubled caller-ID fines. Their profit depends on mass unwanted calling that this bill was designed to deter.

Legitimate telemarketers face added compliance stakes, but the criminal penalties apply only to willful and knowing violations, so honest businesses calling customers legally are largely outside the bill's reach.
